rv.q: The result is one of those priceless evenings that enlarges our understanding while appealing to our emotions.
The Jungle isn't preachy. Instead it proves tense, moving and courageous.

Where 'The Jungle' shines is in showing the clash of world-building optimism and utter desperation behind this contested, now lost patch of Calais: but perhaps its determined comprehensiveness means that these refugees' individual, painful narratives are blurred into one cry of pain.
Joes Murphy and Robertson's vital play The Jungle also does just that, giving a voice and a story to a handful of the thousands of migrants who lived in the infamous Calais camp.

Joe Murphy and Joe Robertson’s unforgettable play The Jungle explores the realities of life in the camp and what drove people to risk their lives to travel thousands of miles to end up on the English Channel seeking asylum in Britain.

Certainly The Jungle is advocacy theatre – certain sections succumb to preachiness – but it's a truly multi-faceted drama about the desperation that drives people to deaden their friendships, still their memories, cut off attachments and become temporary ghosts who pass through hell in order to live again.

cn.t: Critics hail this vital, necessary theatre about the Calais refugee camp as a powerful and humanizing experience. The immersive production and passionate performances vividly recreate lived experience, leaving audiences deeply moved and engaged.
